text: Gate error corrupts the quantum state before you ever measure it — once that's happened, the damage is baked in. Readout error is different: the state itself might be fine, but the classical measurement hardware misreports it some fraction of the time. Because that misreporting follows a known statistical pattern, it can actually be corrected after the fact.

Suppose you characterize a qubit's readout behavior and summarize it as a confusion matrix M, where M of i, j is the probability of measuring i given it was prepared in j. Read column by column: prepared in state 0, you measure 0 ninety-eight percent of the time and 1 two percent of the time. Prepared in state 1, you measure 1 ninety-seven percent of the time and 0 three percent of the time.

If a Hadamard gate produces true probabilities of exactly 0.5 and 0.5, the noisy readout doesn't report those numbers directly — it reports the matrix applied to the truth vector. Instead of a true 50/50 split, you'd observe 0.505 and 0.495, a small but real distortion purely from imperfect measurement, even though the quantum state itself was exactly what you intended.

Here's the key insight: because the distortion is a known, fixed linear transformation, you can undo it by applying the inverse matrix. Applying that inverse to the observed vector recovers 0.5 and 0.5 exactly. This works because readout error happens after the quantum computation is complete — it's a classical post-processing distortion on data you already have, and classical distortions with known statistics can be inverted.

In practice you never observe exact probabilities, only sampled counts. A seeded draw at 4096 shots gives roughly 0.498 and 0.502 instead of exactly 0.505 and 0.495 — additional shot noise layered on top of the readout bias. Applying the inverse to these sampled fractions gives a corrected estimate close to, but not exactly, 0.5 and 0.5. Readout mitigation corrects the systematic bias, but it does not eliminate statistical shot noise — and because matrix inversion can amplify small input variations, the correction can even make the noise component slightly larger.

A single qubit needs only a 2 by 2 calibration matrix, but the matrix grows exponentially with qubit count, so building and inverting it by hand is impractical past a handful of qubits. Real workflows use qiskit-experiments' LocalReadoutError and CorrelatedReadoutError to measure and build these matrices automatically, and for larger qubit counts on real IBM hardware, the dedicated mthree package is the widely used production tool, designed to make readout correction tractable without ever forming the full matrix explicitly.

Next lesson tackles a different kind of error — the kind that accumulates during the circuit itself from imperfect gates — using a technique that estimates the unreachable zero-noise answer by deliberately running with more noise first.
